ref: Autol. 2.10 and 2.15 as discussed by Bethune-Baker (his footnotes cite ad Autol. ii 10-22; the Triad passage 2.15 is not cited in this paragraph)
greek: A very similar view to that of Tatian appears to have been held by Theophilus a little later. He was probably the first to use the actual term Triad (Trinity) and to apply Philo's terms 'indwelling' (or 'immanent') and 'proceeding' (or 'projected' or 'transient') to the Logos. Till God willed to create the world the Logos dwelt in Him, in His inner being, as counsellor - His mind and intelligence - this is the only kind of pre-existence which appears to be recognized, and it is not clear in what way the Logos could be distinguished from the Father.

His essence (ousia [OCR: ova-la]), as it were, rests eternally in God - immanent: his hypostasis is conceived only in the work of revelation.

ref: Autol. 1.7 and 2.10, 2.13, 2.15 (Spirit and Wisdom passages) as Swete discusses them
greek: Theophilus mentions the Holy Spirit by name only in connexion with Creation and Inspiration. The creative Spirit is identified with the Divine Wisdom, and distinguished from the Logos; 'through His Word and His Wisdom God made all things,' as we are taught in Ps. xxxiii. 6. In common with the Word, the Wisdom or Spirit of God issued from God before the world was made. 'God, then, having His own Word within Himself in His own heart, begat Him, causing Him to go forth before the universe in company with His own Wisdom.' In the next sentence indeed the Word is identified with the Spirit, and even with the Spirit of prophecy.

In common with the Word, the Wisdom or Spirit of God issued from God before the world was made. But Theophilus adds: 'the fourth day finds its antitype in Man, who is in need of light; so we get the series, God, the Word, Wisdom, Man.'

ref: Autol. 2.10, 2.15 (Spirit with Logos); Donaldson's general discussion of the Apologists' Spirit
greek: The same generality pervades their treatment of the doctrine of the Holy Spirit. They mention the Spirit in conjunction with the Father and Son as being third in rank. But they seem scarcely to know what to make of the Spirit. Theophilus, and even Justin, speak as if they confounded Him with the Logos. They all recognise his personality in one set of passages and in express assertions, and in another they make Him belong to the Father and to the Son, very much as if He were an attribute.

ref: Autol. 2.15 (Triad: 'Theophilus speaks of the triad'); Donaldson's account of the Logos and Spirit
greek: When Theophilus speaks of the triad, the point of view which he assumes is, that the Logos and Spirit belong to the Father just as a man's mind belongs to the man. In reply to such an explanation a modern thinker would say to Theophilus that he had denied the personality of the Logos and Spirit; but this objection would very likely never have occurred to any ancient theologian at that time, and if it had, it would have been thought a weak one.

ref: Autol. book 1-2 (general); Petavius's reading of Theophilus among ante-Nicene writers

This learned writer, in the second volume of his great work on Theological Doctrines, where he comes to handle the subject of the Trinity (pub. 1644), so expounds the views of the ante-Nicene Fathers, as to establish concerning not a few of them (in particular, Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus, Tertullian, Lactantius, Origen), that they substantially coincided with those of Arius, at least approached nearer to his than to the doctrine of Athanasius.

ref: Autol. 2.10 and 2.22 (Newman's 'Divine gennesis' of the early Fathers, as the literal sense)

what_it_says: Newman states that the early statements, taken literally, tie the Son's gennesis to the creation: the Word is born in order to create.
limits: Newman sets this out as the literal reading he is weighing; it is not his final view, and he treats the Alexandrians as clear of it.

ref: Autol. 2.10 ('the Word ... begat' / 'put forth' passages); Newman's note on the literal sense
greek: There can be no doubt what the literal sense is of words such as these, and that in consequence they require some accommodation in order to reconcile them with the received Catholic teaching de Deo and de SS. Trinitate. It is the object of Bull, as of others after him, to effect this reconciliation.

what_it_says: Newman says the literal sense of such statements needs accommodation to fit Catholic teaching on God and the Trinity, and that Bull set out to supply that accommodation.

ref: Autol. 2.10 (the Word begotten 'before all things'); Newman's list of Fathers holding the view
greek: The opinion which I have been describing is, as far as words go, definitely held by Justin, Tatian, Theophilus, Methodius, in the East; by Hippolytus, Tertullian, Novatian, Lactantius, Zeno, and Victorinus, in the West; and that with so plain an identity of view in these various writers, and with such exact characteristics, that we cannot explain it away into carelessness of writing, personal idiosyncracy, or the influence of some particular school; but are forced to consider it as the common property of them all, so that we may interpret one writer by the other, and illustrate or supply from the rest what is obscure or deficient in each.

what_it_says: Newman says Theophilus is among the writers who, as far as their words go, held the view that the Son's gennesis is tied to creation, and that these writers should be read together.
limits: Newman's 'as far as words go' is a qualifier; he is describing a view he later argues must be read in its 'obvious sense' only with caution.

ref: Autol. 2.10 ('Theos Logos'; the Word and God); Newman's disagreement with Petavius's criticism
greek: There seems no reason then why the words of Theophilus, Hippolytus, and the rest should not be taken in their obvious sense; and so far I agree with Petavius against Bull, Fabricius, Maran, the Ballerini, and Routh. But, this being granted, still I am not disposed to follow Petavius in his severe criticism upon those Fathers, and for the following reasons: 1. They considered the 'Theos Logos' to be really distinct from God, (that is, the Father,) not a mere attribute, quality, or power, as the Sabellians did, and do.

what_it_says: Newman agrees with Petavius that Theophilus's words should be read in their obvious sense, but defends the early writers against Petavius's harsher criticism because they held the Logos to be really distinct from God.
limits: Newman's point 1 is distinctness from God, not an eternal personal Son; the 'obvious sense' concession favours the subordinationist reading he later qualifies.

ref: Autol. 2.15 (the Triad; 'trinitas' term) and the Logos as 'distinct being'
greek: The unity of the Godhead was set forth in the una substantia; the disposition of the one substance among the three Persons (trinitas, τριάς [OCR: 'rptd^'] first by Theophilus) did not destroy the unity (the gnostic eons-speculation is here confined to three in number). [...] But the self-unfolding (not partitioning) of the Godhead had made a beginning (the realization of the world-idea is still ever the main-spring of the inner Divine dispositio); the Logos became a distinct being.
greek_edition: English translation by Edwin Knox Mitchell of Harnack's German (read from archive.org djvu OCR, lines 6105-6120). The Greek 'rptd^' is OCR garbage for τριάς. PDF has no text layer (image-only; pdftotext 3.5 KB for 589 pages), so no PDF page could be checked.
english: The unity of the Godhead was set forth in the una substantia; the disposition of the one substance among the three Persons (trinitas, τριάς [OCR: 'rptd^'] first by Theophilus) did not destroy the unity (the gnostic eons-speculation is here confined to three in number). [...] But the self-unfolding (not partitioning) of the Godhead had made a beginning (the realization of the world-idea is still ever the main-spring of the inner Divine dispositio); the Logos became a distinct being.
translator: Edwin Knox Mitchell (named as translator on the front matter: 'Translated by Edwin Knox Mitchell, M.A.')
edition: Hodder and Stoughton, London, 1893 (archive.org metadata; Harnack, Outlines of the History of Dogma)
what_it_says: Harnack says the term trinitas (τριάς) was first used by Theophilus for the three Persons, and that the Logos became a distinct being through the self-unfolding of the Godhead.
limits: The 'first by Theophilus' note is Harnack's own; Harnack says the Logos became 'a distinct being' after the Godhead's self-unfolding 'had made a beginning', wording that opponents read as a temporal origin.
